```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3.5
)
# ggplot2 is only suggested, so its chunks run only when it is installed.
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r}
library(jacarandr)
```

Each November the jacaranda trees of eastern Australia flower violet, often
next to the orange-red Illawarra flame tree, glossy green figs, lilly pilly
and the last of the golden wattle. jacarandr turns that scene into four
colour palettes.

## The palettes

```{r, fig.height = 3}
jac_show()
```

* **`"main"`**: eight distinct colours for categories. This is the default.
* **`"light"`**: softer versions of the same eight colours, with the same
  names, for large areas or pairing with `"main"`.
* **`"seq"`**: pale petal through jacaranda to deep violet, for ordered
  values.
* **`"div"`**: jacaranda through a near-neutral centre to fig leaf green, for
  values on either side of a meaningful midpoint.

## Getting colours

`jac_pal()` returns hex codes from any palette:

```{r}
jac_pal()
jac_pal("main", n = 4)
jac_pal("seq", n = 6)
```

For the discrete palettes, `n` takes the *first* `n` colours. The order is
chosen so this is always a good subset: the first three (jacaranda, fig leaf
and flame tree) are the most distinct, and each one after adds the most
contrast to those before it. For the continuous palettes, `n` colours are
interpolated evenly in CIELAB space, so any `n` works.

`jac_colours()` picks colours by name, which is useful for highlighting or
for a single accent colour:

```{r}
jac_colours("jacaranda", "flame_tree")
jac_colours("jacaranda", palette = "light")
```

`jac_pal()` returns an unnamed vector on purpose. When a *named* vector is
given to `ggplot2::scale_fill_manual()`, the names are matched to your data
values, so `jac_colours()` output there would leave every bar grey unless
your data happened to contain "jacaranda".

## Reversing

Every function takes `reverse`:

```{r, fig.height = 1.5}
jac_show("main", n = 4, reverse = TRUE)
```

For discrete palettes, the `n` colours are chosen first and then reversed, so
you get the same colours in the opposite order. For continuous palettes, the
palette itself runs the other way, so `"seq"` goes from dark to light.

## Base R graphics

The colours are ordinary hex codes, so they work anywhere:

```{r}
barplot(c(4, 7, 3, 5), col = jac_pal(n = 4), border = NA,
        names.arg = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))
```

```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4}
image(volcano, col = jac_pal("seq", n = 64, reverse = TRUE), axes = FALSE)
```

## ggplot2

The scales follow the common naming pattern: `scale_colour_jac_d()` and
`scale_fill_jac_d()` for discrete data, and `scale_colour_jac_c()` and
`scale_fill_jac_c()` for continuous data. `scale_color_*` spellings also
work.

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mpg, aes(class, fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_jac_d() +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_jac_d(reverse = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The light palette works well for filled shapes with main-coloured outlines:

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, fill = drv, colour = drv)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, size = 3, stroke = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_jac_d(palette = "light") +
  scale_colour_jac_d() +
  theme_minimal()
```

For continuous data:

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2}
ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, fill = density)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_jac_c() +
  theme_minimal()
```

For diverging data, set `midpoint` so the neutral centre colour sits at the
value that matters, usually zero. Without it, the centre colour would fall at
the middle of the data range, which may not be zero at all.

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4}
df <- expand.grid(x = 1:30, y = 1:30)
df$z <- with(df, sin(x / 4) * cos(y / 5) + 0.3)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y, fill = z)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_jac_c(palette = "div", midpoint = 0) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void()
```

### More than eight groups

A discrete palette has 8 colours. With more groups, jacarandr stops with an
error rather than reusing colours (two groups that look identical) or
interpolating new ones (several groups that look nearly identical). Either
group the smaller categories together, or, if the categories have a natural
order, use a continuous palette in the discrete scale:

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2}
ggplot(diamonds, aes(clarity, fill = clarity)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_jac_d(palette = "seq") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Accessibility

Lightness was varied deliberately across the `"main"` colours. For example,
the fig leaf green is clearly darker than the flame tree orange, which keeps
them apart for readers with red-green colour vision deficiency. Every pair of
`"main"` colours is at least 10 CIEDE2000 units apart under simulated
deuteranopia, protanopia and tritanopia, and the package's test suite checks
this. Colour still should not be the only way information is shown: label
lines directly or use shapes too where you can.
